prerequisites: Mathematics I and Mathematics II from scientific-technological baccalaureate, including elementary algebra, trigonometry, and basic calculus.

learning_outcomes.text: Utilize the basic properties of real and complex numbers and perform fundamental operations with them.
Use the basic elements of Linear Algebra: systems of linear equations, vector spaces, and linear applications, and use matrices to simplify their study.
Identify metric properties in vector spaces, through the scalar product, norm, or distance.
Calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors and diagonalize endomorphisms and matrices.
Solve geometric problems in the plane and space.
Identify the basic elements of differential equations and systems of differential equations and use algebraic tools to solve elementary cases.
Ability to solve mathematical problems that may arise in engineering. Aptitude to apply knowledge on: linear algebra.
Knowledge of basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing them with versatility to adapt to new situations.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity and critical reasoning.
Ability to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills and abilities in the field of Industrial Engineering, both orally and in writing, and to all types of audiences.
Honesty, responsibility, ethical commitment and solidarity.
Ability to work in a team.

syllabus_topics: Theme 2. Systems of linear equations and matrices.
2.2. Solving systems using Gauss's Method. Application to the calculation of the inverse matrix.
3.2. Linear combinations and linear independence. Bases and dimension. Coordinates.
4.3. Kernel and image of an application. Classification of linear applications.
5.3. Applications to the resolution of systems of linear differential equations.
6.1. Euclidean vector space. Scalar product and metric properties.
2. Matrix calculus and systems of equations
3. Vector spaces and changes of basis
assessment_rules: The final grade (NF) is calculated as NF = 0.15*NL + maximum (0.15*NA + 0.7*NC, 0.85*NC), where NL is the laboratory practice grade, NA is the classroom practice grade, and NC is the average of the written controls, all out of 10 points. To pass, students must obtain at least 2.5 points out of 10 in each partial control; otherwise, the final grade will be a fail, with a numerical grade of the minimum between NF and 4.5. For differentiated evaluation, if classroom practice attendance is not possible, the formula becomes NF = 0.15*NL + 0.85*NC, with passing conditions of NF ≥ 5, NL ≥ 2.5, and NC ≥ 2.5 in each written exam part. Extraordinary calls involve a written exam (two parts) and a laboratory practice test, using the same grading formula. Grades obtained in classroom practices are conserved for all calls of the same academic year; laboratory practice grades can be conserved or replaced by a specific exam.
